checks.covers: Components of the lockfiles and manifests that carry a published advisory in the OSV database, the sign that a component was left behind.
checks.misses: The documented update and remediation time frames themselves (a person's policy), components with no published advisory, and anything resolved only at install or deploy time.

checks.covers: Components of the lockfiles and manifests that carry a published vulnerability, with the fixed version when there is one.
checks.misses: The documented time frames for updates (they are a person's policy), components with no published advisory, and packages added at build or deploy time.

checks.covers: Go modules with a published vulnerability whose vulnerable function the program actually reaches.
checks.misses: The documented update time frames, vulnerable modules the call analysis cannot prove reachable, and non-Go components.

checks.covers: Rust crates of Cargo.lock listed in the RustSec advisory database, yanked crates included.
checks.misses: The documented update time frames, crates with no advisory yet, and non-Rust components.

checks.covers: NuGet packages, direct and transitive, that the .NET tooling reports as vulnerable.
checks.misses: The documented update time frames, packages with no advisory, and anything outside NuGet.

entries.why: A component with a published advisory that is still in the project is the visible sign of a breached remediation window. The tools find the advisory, not the project's own deadline, so each check is partial.

checks.covers: axios requests made without a timeout, which wait forever by default and let one stalled server hold the work.
checks.misses: Other HTTP clients (fetch, got, node-fetch), a timeout set by a shared client factory or an interceptor, and every other time-consuming or resource-hungry function.

checks.covers: Outbound HTTP calls of the common Python client libraries made without a timeout argument.
checks.misses: A timeout set on a session, an adapter or a wrapper defined elsewhere, other libraries, and every other resource-demanding function.

checks.covers: Go HTTP clients and calls built without a timeout, where the default client waits forever.
checks.misses: A deadline carried by a context passed through several functions, a shared client built elsewhere, and every other resource-demanding function.

checks.covers: Java outbound clients (the JDK HttpClient, RestTemplate, Apache HttpClient, HttpURLConnection) built or used without a timeout.
checks.misses: Timeouts configured through a shared bean or container settings, other clients, and every other resource-demanding function.

checks.covers: PHP outbound HTTP calls made without a timeout option.
checks.misses: A timeout set in the client's shared configuration, php.ini limits, and every other resource-demanding function.

checks.covers: reqwest clients and calls, blocking and async, built without a timeout.
checks.misses: A timeout set on the request elsewhere than the same expression, other clients, and every other resource-demanding function.

entries.why: An outbound call that never times out is one concrete way a slow dependency exhausts the service's workers, which this item guards against. The rules see only that case; rate limits, size limits and queue bounds stay outside.

checks.covers: Resolver settings, source priority and lockfile use that let a package name resolve from an unintended registry.
checks.misses: Registry-side controls and transitive dependencies resolved only at install time.

checks.covers: Lockfile entries of npm and Python that resolve from a registry host outside the trusted list, from a git or URL source, or with no integrity hash, which is where a name can be taken by another party.
checks.misses: Registry-side controls such as namespace reservation, ecosystems with no lockfile reader (only npm and Python lockfiles are read), and resolver settings outside the lockfiles.

checks.covers: CI workflow references to actions that are not pinned to an immutable commit, or whose reference can be read as a branch or a tag, the pipeline form of a source the name does not fix.
checks.misses: Package resolution inside the build steps, registries chosen by the runner's environment, and the audits that need the GitHub API (they run only when the instance turns offline mode off).

entries.why: The ledger block reads the resolver configuration; the supply-chain tool reads the lockfiles for sources and integrity that leave a name open to substitution, and the workflow audit does the same for pipeline references. Identifiers for supply-chain were read in the adapter's analyzer (src/adapters/supply-chain/analyze.ts); those for zizmor come from the audit names in its documentation of the pinned range and were not seen in a recorded report here, so the review has to confirm them.

checks.covers: Python serializers or model forms declared to output every field of a model, so a column added later is returned unreviewed.
checks.misses: Handlers that return a model object directly, serializers whose field list is built dynamically, and fields that are listed but should not be.

checks.covers: Jackson configured to see every field of a model, private ones included.
checks.misses: Entities returned straight from a controller with default visibility, other serialization libraries, and listed fields that should stay private.

checks.covers: PHP resources or serializers declared to output the whole model.
checks.misses: Models returned directly as JSON, a hidden-attribute list that is too short, and other frameworks.

entries.why: Returning every field of a data object is the exact shape of returning more than the caller needs. The rules find the declared-all form only, so the check is partial.

checks.covers: Server-side fetches of caller-influenced URLs, including how redirects are followed.
checks.misses: Fixed trusted URLs whose redirect setting is a plain client option, and HTTP clients configured outside the repository.

checks.covers: PHP outbound requests whose address comes from request data while redirect following is left on, the default of Guzzle and the Laravel HTTP client.
checks.misses: Other PHP HTTP clients, addresses that reach the call through another function, and every other language.

entries.why: The audit block follows redirect handling in fetches, and the rule marks the PHP case where the address is caller-chosen and redirects stay enabled.

checks.covers: Request-body fields that override what the permission model meant to restrict, the pattern of binding client input straight to a stored object.
checks.misses: Every framework binding feature by name; it is a model's reading, not a rule per framework.

checks.covers: A model created or updated from the whole request body in JavaScript and TypeScript.
checks.misses: A body copied into a variable first, ORMs other than the ones the rule names, and fields filtered by a middleware.

checks.covers: Model schemas that accept fields they do not declare, so request data can store any field.
checks.misses: Schemas built dynamically, validation done before the model, and ORMs the rule does not model.

checks.covers: Models built or updated from the whole request body and forms declared open to every field.
checks.misses: Dictionaries unpacked after passing through a function, allow-lists applied elsewhere, and frameworks not modeled.

checks.covers: TryUpdateModelAsync or UpdateModel used without a list of allowed properties.
checks.misses: Entities bound as action parameters, DTOs that carry sensitive fields, and binder attributes declared on the model.

checks.covers: Beans filled from the whole request parameter map, or a data binder whose default protection is cleared.
checks.misses: Binding through annotations on the entity, DTOs with sensitive fields, and frameworks other than the ones modeled.

checks.covers: Models filled from the whole request, or declared open to every attribute.
checks.misses: A fillable list that is too wide, guarded models that are filled with unvetted keys elsewhere, and other frameworks.

entries.why: The audit block asks whether a body field can change what the action did not mean to change, and the rules name the construct that binds the whole request to a model, in six languages.

checks.covers: Trust placed in forwarded-address headers and how the application derives the client address from them.
checks.misses: The proxy and web server configuration outside the repository, and how the chain is deployed.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in JavaScript and TypeScript handlers.
checks.misses: A trust-proxy setting that makes the header safe, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in Python request handlers.
checks.misses: A trusted-proxy middleware that makes the header safe, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in C# handlers.
checks.misses: The forwarded-headers middleware configured for known proxies, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in Go handlers.
checks.misses: A trusted-proxy setting in the router, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in Java handlers.
checks.misses: A container configured to rewrite the address for known proxies, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in PHP code.
checks.misses: Trusted proxies configured in the framework, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

checks.covers: The client address read straight from a forwarding header in Rust handlers.
checks.misses: A proxy that overwrites the header before it reaches the program, the address passing through a helper, and the proxy chain itself.

entries.why: The audit block treats forwarded-address headers as trust decisions, and the rules mark the read of such a header as the client address in each language, which is the part of the item a pattern can see.

checks.covers: A hash, token or password compared with PHP's type-juggling equality, where a string that looks like a number can match another.
checks.misses: Loose comparisons of values the rule does not name as secrets, type confusion in other languages, and checks of variable types before use.

entries.why: Type juggling in a comparison is the named weakness, and PHP is where the language makes it the default behaviour of the equality operator. Other languages need their own rules and stay outside.

checks.covers: Recursive merges and path writes that let an attacker-chosen key reach prototype state, with the gadget that uses it.
checks.misses: JavaScript that is never reached by this reading, and a defensive style (such as using maps) that is absent but harmless.

checks.covers: A property name taken from the request that is used to reach into an object and assign a value, with no check of the reserved names.
checks.misses: Names that reach the write through another function, key checks written in a form the rule does not recognize, and server code that is not JavaScript.

checks.covers: Hand-written recursive merges that copy every key of their source without skipping the reserved names.
checks.misses: Merge functions of libraries (their versions are a dependency question), merges using another loop shape, and merges into objects without a prototype.

entries.why: Prototype pollution exists in JavaScript and TypeScript only; the audit block and the two rules look for the write and the unguarded merge that cause it.

checks.covers: An AI reading of the source for places where a parameter can arrive from several sources (query, body, cookie, header) with no rule on which one wins.
checks.misses: What the framework or a proxy does with repeated parameters at run time, and code the model did not read.

entries.why: No pattern tells which source a framework prefers for a repeated parameter; reading how handlers pick their inputs is a judgment the AI review can make and a person must still check.

checks.covers: Shared caches, lazy initialization and teardown reached by concurrent paths without a guard.
checks.misses: Races that need a schedule the reading cannot show; the block is written for native targets and reads less well on managed runtimes.

entries.why: The audit block looks for state shared between concurrent paths that lacks the guard, which is the weakness this item names.

checks.covers: Races between a check and the use on file operations.
checks.misses: Permission checks followed by a separate action on non-file resources.

checks.covers: Checks on state that concurrent paths can invalidate before use.
checks.misses: Races without a security-relevant state change, which the block leaves unconfirmed.

entries.why: Both audit blocks name the gap between a check and its use as the thing to hunt.

checks.covers: Inconsistent lock acquisition order and locks held across callbacks or blocking calls.
checks.misses: Where lock logic lives (whether outside code can alter it) and cases that cannot be triggered by bounded input.

entries.why: The audit block hunts deadlocks from lock ordering, which is the stuck-thread half of this item.

checks.covers: Shared pools and locks where one workload holds a slot others need.
checks.misses: Whether thread pools or priorities are used by design, which this block does not judge.

entries.why: The audit block looks for starvation of shared workers, the failure this item guards against.
